First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+{x}^{2}/2)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this integral now resembles the basic integral for the inverse tangent,

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\,\textrm d u = \arctan{u} + C.
$$

We make the substitution $u=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt 2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt 2 \,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡u|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡1-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2}\frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{\sqrt{2}/2} \\  & =2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)-2\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $14$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We can often use this trick whenever we see an integral that closely resembles an integral for an inverse trigonometric function.

**Note:** As always, after solving an integral using substitution, we should always double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x)]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $9x^2 = (3x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \,\textrm d u=\textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{4\sqrt{1-9{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x)^{2}}}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{12}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Note that we can rewrite this integral as

$$
\int \dfrac{3}{2 + 50x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{3}{2(1 + 25x^2)} = \dfrac 3 2 \int \dfrac{1}{1+25x^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+u^2}\textrm{d}u =\arctan u +C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $25x^2 = (5x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 5\,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{2+50{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+25{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+(5x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\,\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡5x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+{x}^{2}/2)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2(1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{1+(x/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that this integral now resembles the basic integral for the inverse tangent,

$$
\int\dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\,\textrm d u = \arctan{u} + C.
$$

We make the substitution $u=\dfrac{x}{\sqrt 2}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sqrt 2 \,\textrm d u = \textrm d x.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\sqrt2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡u|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡1-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for $\textrm{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

Let $u = 5x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
5\,\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5\,\text{d}x}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(5x)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
In this lesson, we learned how to use substitution to evaluate integrals that give rise to inverse trigonometric functions.

Although you can always solve these integrals by going through the substitution process, it is convenient to remember the following key results:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(ax)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{a}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{1+(ax)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(ax)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{{a}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)+C \\ \int \frac{1}{|ax|\sqrt{(ax)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{a}\text{arcsec}(ax)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To remember the results above, note the following:

- Whenever the integrand has an $ax$ term, the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $ax.$

- Otherwise, if the $a$ and $x$ are separated, then the argument of the resulting inverse trigonometric function is $\dfrac{x}{a}.$

- All the results are multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{a},$ except for $\arcsin \left( \dfrac{x}{a} \right) + C.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \text{d}u & =2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^2+1.$

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline x & -1 & 0 \\ \hline u & 2 & 1 \\ \hline\end{array}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^0 x(x^2+1)^3\,\textrm{d}x=\int_2^1 u^3\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}{|}_{2}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{1}^{4}-{2}^{4}}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1-16}{4} \\  & =-\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Important**: Note that in this example, when we changed the limits the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 \ldots \textrm{d}x
$$ became $$
\displaystyle \int_{2}^1 \ldots \textrm{d}u.
$$ When changing the limits, it is important to respect the order in which the limits are applied. The lower limit of the integral in $u$ must correspond to the lower limit of the integral in $x.$ Same for the upper limit.

We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{3}+2 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2} \\ \text{d}u & =3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & ={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^3+2.$

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline x & -1 & 2 \\ \hline u & 1 & 10 \\ \hline\end{array}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^2 \dfrac{1}{(x^3+2)}\,x^2\textrm{d}x=\int_1^{10} \dfrac{1}{u}\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(10).\end{aligned}
$$
